proposed.subtitle:
Respiration: what it is, where it happens, and the two pathways

­ƒôÿ Say it cleanly: respiration is an exothermic chemical process in cells that transfers energy from glucose for life processes ÔÇö it is not breathing.

- --

­ƒôÿ The key idea is:

Aerobic respiration uses oxygen to fully oxidise glucose ÔåÆ lots of ATP; anaerobic uses no oxygen ÔåÆ incomplete breakdown ÔåÆ less ATP + specific products.

What happens in cells:

  • Aerobic (mainly in mitochondria): glucose + oxygen ÔåÆ carbon dioxide + water (+ energy transferred).
  • Anaerobic in animals (cytoplasm): glucose ÔåÆ lactic acid (+ small energy transfer).
  • Anaerobic in yeast/plants (fermentation): glucose ÔåÆ ethanol + carbon dioxide.

Why cells need the energy:

  • Build larger molecules (e.g. proteins).
  • Muscle contraction for movement.
  • Thermoregulation to keep enzymes at suitable temperature.

Structure ÔåÆ function / Process ÔåÆ effect:

  • Mitochondria have folded inner membranes ÔåÆ Ôåæ surface for enzymes ÔåÆ faster aerobic ATP transfer.
  • During hard exercise, oxygen supply cannot meet demand ÔåÆ cells switch to anaerobic ÔåÆ lactic acid accumulates ÔåÆ oxygen debt after exercise to oxidise it.

proposed.title: CORE LEARNING
proposed.subtitle:
Metabolism: the cellÔÇÖs economy

LetÔÇÖs ensure every label you use earns you marks.

­ƒôÿ Central idea

Catabolism involves breaking down molecules and releasing energy; anabolism involves building larger molecules and utilizing that energy. The energy is released during respiration and is transferred to reactions by ATP.

What actually happens

  • After digestion, cells receive glucose, fatty acids + glycerol, and amino acids.
  • Glucose is broken down in aerobic respiration (primarily in mitochondria) ÔåÆ energy is released ÔåÆ this energy is transferred by ATP.
  • ATP then drives anabolic reactions:
    • Glucose ÔåÆ glycogen (in animals) / starch & cellulose (in plants)
    • Glycerol + 3 fatty acids ÔåÆ lipid (triglyceride)
    • Amino acids ÔåÆ proteins
  • Plants also synthesize amino acids from glucose + nitrates ÔåÆ and subsequently build proteins.
  • Excess amino acids undergo deamination in the liver ÔåÆ ammonia is converted to urea ÔåÆ the kidneys excrete urea in urine.

Structure ÔåÆ function / Process ÔåÆ effect

  • Specific enzymes (with active sites) ÔåÆ catalyse only certain reactions ÔåÆ allowing reactions to proceed rapidly at body temperature.
  • Mitochondria ÔåÆ the primary site of aerobic respiration ÔåÆ yielding high amounts of ATP ÔåÆ which fuels biosynthesis.
  • Liver ÔåÆ contains enzymes for deamination ÔåÆ converting toxic ammonia into urea for safe excretion.

­ƒÆí Why this matters

  • It clarifies where energy originates for building and repairing tissues.
  • It connects diet to storage (glycogen/lipids) and to waste (urea).

Common slip to avoid: Respiration refers to a chemical reaction in cells; breathing is the physical movement of air in and out of the lungs.

  • ATP then drives anabolic reactions:
    • Glucose ÔåÆ glycogen (in animals) / starch & cellulose (in plants)
    • Glycerol + 3 fatty acids ÔåÆ lipid (triglyceride)
    • Amino acids ÔåÆ proteins
  • Plants also synthesize amino acids from glucose + nitrates ÔåÆ and subsequently build proteins.
  • Excess amino acids undergo deamination in the liver ÔåÆ ammonia is converted to urea ÔåÆ the kidneys excrete urea in urine.

Structure ÔåÆ function / Process ÔåÆ effect

  • Specific enzymes (with active sites) ÔåÆ catalyse only certain reactions ÔåÆ allowing reactions to proceed rapidly at body temperature.
  • Mitochondria ÔåÆ the primary site of aerobic respiration ÔåÆ yielding high amounts of ATP ÔåÆ which fuels biosynthesis.
  • Liver ÔåÆ contains enzymes for deamination ÔåÆ converting toxic ammonia into urea for safe excretion.

­ƒÆí Why this matters

  • It clarifies where energy originates for building and repairing tissues.
  • It connects diet to storage (glycogen/lipids) and to waste (urea).

Common slip to avoid: Respiration refers to a chemical reaction in cells; breathing is the physical movement of air in and out of the lungs.
